title: Walking pilgrimage
hookLine: the Camino to Santiago, Lourdes, Jerusalem: walking as prayer

lines: A SCALLOP SHELL ON A BACKPACK.
A BOOKLET STAMPED ALONG THE WAY.
cards: Tied to the back of a dusty backpack, a scallop shell bounces with every step. The person wearing it has blisters, a walking stick, and a little booklet that gets stamped in towns along the way.
Ahead are more days of the same: up early, walk, eat, sleep in a bunk room full of strangers, walk again.

The road is the Camino, the Way of Saint James, and it ends at a cathedral in Santiago, in the northwest corner of Spain. Ask walkers why they're doing it, and the answers run all over the place. Grief.

teach.b: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, made as an act of devotion. Christians walk to many such places; here are three, and the thread that runs through them. First, Santiago.
Tradition says the apostle James is buried there, and pilgrims walk to his tomb, some wearing the scallop shell as their sign. Second, Lourdes, in the south of France.

teach.h: LOURDES: THE GROTTO AND THE SPRING.
teach.b: Catholic tradition holds that Mary appeared there to a young girl named Bernadette, beside a grotto with a spring. Pilgrims come to pray, to bathe in the water, and to bring the sick.

Third, Jerusalem. Christian pilgrims walk the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrows, stopping to pray at stations along the route Jesus is remembered to have carried his cross. And the thread runs back into the Bible.
Its Book of Psalms has a group of songs headed "A Song of degrees," which some readers take as songs for going up to Jerusalem.
One of them begins: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD."
And then: "Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem." Our feet. Not our thoughts.
On a pilgrimage the body does the praying: the distance, the weather, the ache in the legs, the strangers who share bread.

teach.h: I WAS GLAD WHEN THEY SAID UNTO ME.
teach.b: Some walkers say the arrival matters less than they expected, and the road matters more. Prayer doesn't have to sit still. Here it gets up and walks.

how: Christian pilgrims walk routes like the Camino to Santiago, often carrying a stamped pilgrim's credential, and visit places like Lourdes and Jerusalem to pray, attend Mass or services, and walk the stations of the cross.

o: a journey on foot to a holy place, made as prayer
a long hike taken for fitness and fresh air
a march held to mark the founding of a town

p: tradition says James is buried there
the way of sorrows in Jerusalem
psalms some read as pilgrim songs

s: on the Camino, some pilgrims wear a scallop shell
the shell is the sign of the road to Santiago, tied to backpacks along the way.
a pilgrimage only counts once you arrive
on a walking pilgrimage the road itself is the prayer: the distance, the weather, the strangers.
the Via Dolorosa is a road to Santiago
it's in Jerusalem: the way of sorrows, where pilgrims stop at stations along the route of the cross.

games.q: you're a pilgrim with a scallop shell, a stamped booklet and sore feet, many days from Santiago. what keeps you walking?
o: only the cathedral at the end.
the road itself: the walking is the prayer.
games.why: some walkers say the arrival matters less than they expected, and the road more. the psalm says: our feet shall stand within thy gates.

practice: Choose a destination close by, a window, a doorway, a plant, a tree outside, and before you set off, name one thing you're carrying: a hope, a worry, a person.
Walk to it slowly, the way you'd walk the last stretch to a cathedral, feeling each foot land. When you arrive, stay there; if you pray, offer what you carried, and if not, just let yourself arrive.

wordCard.voice: Walking pilgrimage. A journey on foot to a holy place, Santiago, Lourdes, Jerusalem, where the walking itself becomes the prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a song of ascents, the heading the King James Bible gives as "a song of degrees."

carryVoice: Your line: walking as prayer. Our feet shall stand within thy gates. See you tomorrow.
